title: Modern Periodic Table — Groups, Periods & Trends
answer: The Modern Periodic Table organizes 118 confirmed chemical elements into 18 vertical Groups and 7 horizontal Periods in order of increasing atomic number (Z), formulated by Henry Moseley in 1913. Elements in the same group possess identical valence electron configurations and similar chemical reactivities.
highlights: Group 1 (Alkali Metals: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr): Highly reactive, 1 valence electron (ns¹), form +1 cations
Group 2 (Alkaline Earth Metals: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra): 2 valence electrons (ns²), form +2 cations
Groups 3–12 (Transition Metals / d-block): Variable oxidation states, form colored ions and complexes, act as catalysts
Group 16 (Chalcogens / Oxygen Family: O, S, Se, Te, Po)
Group 17 (Halogens: F, Cl, Br, I, At): Highly electronegative salt-formers, 7 valence electrons (ns²np⁵), form -1 halide anions
Group 18 (Noble Gases: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn): Chemically inert with complete octet (ns²np⁶, except He with 1s² duplet)
Periodic Trends: Electronegativity and Ionization Energy increase across a period (left to right) and decrease down a group; Atomic Radius decreases across a period and increases down a group

title: Major Classes of Chemical Reactions
answer: Fundamental chemical reaction types include: Combination (A + B → AB), Decomposition (AB → A + B), Single Displacement (A + BC → AC + B), Double Displacement / Precipitation (AB + CD → AD + CB), Redox (simultaneous oxidation and reduction via electron transfer), Esterification (Carboxylic Acid + Alcohol ⇌ Ester + Water), and Saponification (Alkaline hydrolysis of fats into soap and glycerol).
highlights: Combination: 2 Mg + O₂ → 2 MgO (Two or more reactants combine to form a single product)
Decomposition: 2 FeSO₄ + Heat → Fe₂O₃ + SO₂↑ + SO₃↑; 2 Pb(NO₃)₂ + Heat → 2 PbO + 4 NO₂↑ (brown fumes) + O₂↑
Displacement: Fe + CuSO₄(aq, blue) → FeSO₄(aq, light green) + Cu(s, reddish-brown)
Esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH (in presence of conc. H₂SO₄) ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ (Ethyl Acetate, fruity sweet aroma) + H₂O
Saponification: Fat/Triglyceride + 3 NaOH → Glycerol + 3 Soap molecules (Sodium salts of fatty acids)

title: Buffer Solutions & The Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation
answer: A buffer solution resists changes in its pH upon the addition of small quantities of an acid or a base. For an acidic buffer (weak acid + its conjugate salt, e.g., CH₃COOH + CH₃COONa), the pH is calculated via the Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation: pH = pK_a + log₁₀([Salt] / [Acid]).
highlights: Henderson-Hasselbalch Equation (Acidic Buffer): pH = pK_a + log₁₀([A⁻] / [HA]) = pK_a + log₁₀([Conjugate Base / Salt] / [Weak Acid])
Basic Buffer Formula: pOH = pK_b + log₁₀([Conjugate Acid / Salt] / [Weak Base]), and pH = 14 - pOH at 25 °C (e.g., NH₄OH + NH₄Cl)
Blood Buffer System: Human blood maintains a tight physiological pH of 7.35–7.45 using the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system (H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻)

title: Grignard Reagents (RMgX) — Organometallic Synthesis
answer: A Grignard reagent is an organomagnesium compound with the general formula R-Mg-X (where R is an alkyl/aryl group and X is a halogen), synthesized by reacting an organic halide with magnesium metal in anhydrous diethyl ether. Discovered by François Auguste Victor Grignard (1912 Nobel Prize in Chemistry), it serves as an exceptionally strong carbon nucleophile (carbanion source).
highlights: Preparation: R-X + Mg (in dry ether / THF) → R-Mg-X
Synthesis of Alcohols: 1) Formaldehyde (HCHO) + RMgX → 1° Primary Alcohol; 2) Other Aldehydes (R'CHO) + RMgX → 2° Secondary Alcohol; 3) Ketones (R'COR'') + RMgX → 3° Tertiary Alcohol
Reaction with CO₂: RMgX + CO₂ → R-COOMgX → (H₃O⁺) → R-COOH (Carboxylic Acid)
Moisture Sensitivity: Reacts instantly with water, alcohols, or any acidic proton to yield alkanes (R-Mg-X + H₂O → R-H + Mg(OH)X)

title: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) in Benzene
answer: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS) is the fundamental reaction mechanism where an electrophile (E⁺) replaces a hydrogen atom on an aromatic benzene ring, preserving the stable aromatic π-electron sextet (Hückel's 4n+2 rule). Major EAS reactions include Nitration, Halogenation, Sulfonation, Friedel-Crafts Alkylation, and Friedel-Crafts Acylation.
highlights: Nitration: Benzene + conc. HNO₃ + conc. H₂SO₄ (50–60 °C) → Nitrobenzene + H₂O (Electrophile is Nitronium ion: NO₂⁺)
Halogenation: Benzene + Cl₂ (in presence of anhydrous FeCl₃ or AlCl₃ Lewis acid catalyst) → Chlorobenzene + HCl (Electrophile: Cl⁺)
Friedel-Crafts Alkylation: Benzene + CH₃Cl (anh. AlCl₃) → Toluene + HCl (Electrophile: Carbocation CH₃⁺)
Friedel-Crafts Acylation: Benzene + CH₃COCl (anh. AlCl₃) → Acetophenone + HCl (Electrophile: Acylium ion CH₃-C⁺=O)

Activating vs Deactivating Groups: -OH, -NH₂, -OCH₃, -CH₃ are ortho/para-directing activators; -NO₂, -COOH, -CHO, -SO₃H are meta-directing deactivators (Halogens are deactivating but ortho/para-directing due to resonance)

title: Periodic Table Trends — Radius, IE, and Electronegativity
answer: Across a Period (left to right): Atomic radius decreases (effective nuclear charge Z_eff increases), Ionization Energy increases, Electronegativity increases (Fluorine is most electronegative at 4.0 on Pauling scale). Down a Group (top to bottom): Atomic radius increases (new shells added), Ionization Energy decreases, Electronegativity decreases (Francium/Cesium are least electronegative).
highlights: Most electronegative element: Fluorine (F, 4.0) > Oxygen (O, 3.5) > Nitrogen (N, 3.0) ≈ Chlorine (Cl, 3.0)
Highest electron gain enthalpy (electron affinity): Chlorine (Cl, -349 kJ/mol, higher than F due to less inter-electronic repulsion)
Highest first ionization energy: Helium (He, 2372 kJ/mol)
Lanthanide Contraction: Steady decrease in ionic radii across lanthanides due to poor shielding by 4f electrons, making 4d and 5d transition series (e.g. Zr/Hf) nearly identical in size

title: VSEPR Theory and Orbital Hybridization
answer: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory predicts 3D molecular geometry based on minimizing electrostatic repulsion between electron pairs: Lone Pair-Lone Pair > Lone Pair-Bond Pair > Bond Pair-Bond Pair. Hybridization combines atomic orbitals into equivalent hybrid orbitals: sp (linear, 180°), sp² (trigonal planar, 120°), sp³ (tetrahedral, 109.5°), sp³d (trigonal bipyramidal), sp³d² (octahedral, 90°).
highlights: CH₄ (Methane): sp³ hybridized, 0 lone pairs → Perfect Tetrahedral, 109.5° bond angle
NH₃ (Ammonia): sp³ hybridized, 1 lone pair → Trigonal Pyramidal, 107° bond angle (repulsion compresses angle)
H₂O (Water): sp³ hybridized, 2 lone pairs → Bent / V-shaped, 104.5° bond angle
PCl₅: sp³d hybridized → Trigonal Bipyramidal with axial bonds longer than equatorial bonds; SF₆: sp³d² → Octahedral (all bonds 90°)

answer: Water (H₂O, molar mass 18.015 g/mol) is a polar molecule with bent geometry (104.5° bond angle) and extensive hydrogen bonding.
